title: 38 CFR Part 3 - Adjudication
description: The official VA regulations governing how disability claims are processed, evaluated, and decided. Understanding these rules empowers veterans to file stronger claims and effectively appeal unfavorable decisions.

revisionInfo.source: eCFR - Title 38: Pensions, Bonuses, and Veterans' Relief

categories.title: Key Definitions (§3.1)
categories.description: Official VA definitions that determine how your claim is processed

regulations.title: Claim
regulations.summary: A written or electronic communication requesting a determination of entitlement to a specific benefit under VA laws, submitted on an application form prescribed by the Secretary.
keyPoints: Must be on official VA forms (like VA Form 21-526EZ for disability compensation)
Electronic submissions through VA.gov are valid claims
Identifies the veteran and the benefit sought
regulations.veteranTip: Always use official VA forms. Informal statements or letters are NOT claims - they may trigger VA's duty to send you the proper form, but won't protect your effective date.

regulations.title: Initial Claim
regulations.summary: Any complete claim, other than a supplemental claim, for a benefit on a form prescribed by the Secretary. The first initial claim received is called an 'original claim.'
keyPoints: Includes new claims requesting service connection
Includes claims for increased ratings
The first claim you ever file is your 'original claim'
regulations.veteranTip: Your original claim date can be preserved for years through proper Intent to File and appeal procedures.

regulations.title: Supplemental Claim
regulations.summary: A complete claim for VA benefits where an initial or supplemental claim for the same or similar benefit was previously decided.
keyPoints: Must include new and relevant evidence
Filed on VA Form 20-0995
One path to reopen a previously denied claim
regulations.veteranTip: If you have new evidence (like a nexus letter or buddy statements), a supplemental claim is often your best path after a denial.

categories.title: Benefit of the Doubt (§3.102)
categories.description: The legal standard that tilts the scales in your favor

regulations.title: Reasonable Doubt
regulations.summary: When the evidence is in approximate balance (50/50), the benefit of the doubt goes to the veteran. VA will give the benefit of the doubt to the veteran.
keyPoints: You do NOT need to prove your case beyond a reasonable doubt
You do NOT need a preponderance (more than 50%) of evidence
If evidence is roughly equal for and against, YOU WIN
This applies to service connection, ratings, and effective dates
regulations.veteranTip: This is one of your most powerful protections! If your evidence is 'at least as likely as not' (50% probability), you should win. Cite §3.102 in appeals if VA ignored this standard.
regulations.importantQuote: When there is an approximate balance of positive and negative evidence regarding any issue material to the determination of a matter, the Secretary shall give the benefit of the doubt to the claimant.

categories.title: Your Rights as a Claimant (§3.103)
categories.description: Due process protections every veteran should know

regulations.title: Statement of Policy
regulations.summary: Every claimant has the right to written notice of decisions, the right to a hearing, and the right of representation. VA must assist you in developing facts and grant every benefit supported by law.
keyPoints: VA must provide written notice of ALL decisions
You have the right to a hearing
You can have representation (VSO, attorney, agent)
VA proceedings are 'ex parte' - VA must help you, not work against you
regulations.veteranTip: VA is supposed to work WITH you, not against you. They have a duty to grant 'every benefit that can be supported in law.' If they're being adversarial, cite this regulation.
regulations.importantQuote: Proceedings before VA are ex parte in nature, and it is the obligation of VA to assist a claimant in developing the facts pertinent to the claim and to render a decision which grants every benefit that can be supported in law.

regulations.title: Right to Notice
regulations.summary: Claimants and representatives are entitled to notice of any decision affecting benefits, including the issues adjudicated, evidence considered, applicable laws, favorable findings, and what's needed for higher ratings.
keyPoints: Decision letters must identify all issues decided
Must summarize the evidence considered
Must explain applicable laws and regulations
Must list favorable findings that cannot be reversed
Must explain what's needed to get the next higher rating
regulations.veteranTip: Your rating decision letter should tell you EXACTLY what evidence you need for a higher rating. If it doesn't, the decision may be inadequate.

regulations.title: Submission of Evidence
regulations.summary: VA must include in the record ALL evidence submitted by the claimant in support of a pending claim. The evidentiary record closes when VA issues notice of a decision.
keyPoints: VA must consider ALL evidence you submit before a decision
Once a decision is issued, you need to file a review option to add new evidence
Evidence received after a decision requires a supplemental claim or Board appeal
regulations.veteranTip: Submit ALL your evidence BEFORE VA decides your claim. If you have more evidence after a decision, file a supplemental claim promptly.

regulations.title: Right to a Hearing
regulations.summary: Upon request, you are entitled to a hearing on any issue before VA issues a decision. Hearings are held at VA regional offices or via video.
keyPoints: You can request a hearing before any initial or supplemental claim decision
No hearing available for Higher-Level Review (HLR)
Board of Veterans Appeals offers optional hearings
Can be in-person or video teleconference
regulations.veteranTip: Hearings are optional but can be powerful. You can explain your symptoms, clarify evidence, and make your case directly to a decision-maker.

categories.title: Final Decisions & Errors (§3.104-§3.105)
categories.description: When decisions become final and how to correct errors

regulations.title: Binding Nature of Decisions
regulations.summary: A decision by VA is binding on all VA field offices and final after the review period expires, unless appealed or shown to contain clear and unmistakable error.
keyPoints: Decisions become final if not appealed within the timeframe
Review options: Supplemental Claim, Higher-Level Review, or Board Appeal
Modern review system gives 1 year to choose a review option
regulations.veteranTip: You have 1 year from a decision to choose a review option without losing your effective date. Don't let that deadline pass!

regulations.title: Favorable Findings
regulations.summary: Any favorable finding made by a VA adjudicator is binding on all subsequent adjudicators, unless clear and unmistakable error is shown.
keyPoints: If VA found an in-service event occurred, they cannot reverse that later
Favorable findings carry forward to future claims
Can only be reversed if there was clear and unmistakable error
regulations.veteranTip: If VA previously acknowledged your in-service injury, that finding is locked in! Future adjudicators must honor it.

regulations.title: Clear and Unmistakable Error (CUE)
regulations.summary: Final decisions can be revised if there was clear and unmistakable error - meaning the correct facts were known but the law was incorrectly applied, and the outcome would undoubtedly have been different.
keyPoints: Very high standard - must be 'undebatable' that error occurred
Correct facts must have been in the record at the time
Law must have been incorrectly applied
Outcome must have been manifestly different but for the error
If successful, can get back-pay to the original effective date
regulations.veteranTip: CUE claims are difficult but powerful. If you believe VA made an obvious error years ago, a successful CUE claim can result in substantial back-pay.

regulations.title: Reduction in Evaluation
regulations.summary: Before reducing a disability rating, VA must notify you and allow 60 days to submit evidence showing the reduction is not warranted.
keyPoints: VA must send a proposed reduction letter
You get 60 days to respond with evidence
You can request a hearing
Certain ratings have additional protections (see §3.344)
regulations.veteranTip: Never ignore a proposed reduction letter! Respond with medical evidence showing your condition hasn't improved, and request a hearing if needed.

categories.title: How to File Claims (§3.155-§3.160)
categories.description: The rules for properly filing and protecting your claim date

regulations.title: Intent to File
regulations.summary: You can reserve your effective date for up to 1 year by submitting an Intent to File (ITF), giving you time to gather evidence.
keyPoints: Can be submitted electronically, on VA Form 21-0966, or verbally to VA
Reserves your effective date for 12 months
Must file complete claim within 1 year to preserve the date
Does NOT need to identify specific conditions
regulations.veteranTip: ALWAYS file an Intent to File first! If your claim takes months to prepare, you'll get back-pay from the ITF date, not the final claim date. This can be worth thousands of dollars.

regulations.title: Complete Claim Requirement
regulations.summary: A complete claim is required for benefits. VA will consider entitlement to ancillary benefits and secondary conditions as part of your claim.
keyPoints: Must use prescribed VA forms
VA will adjudicate ancillary benefits automatically (SMC, DEA, etc.)
VA considers complications listed in the rating criteria
Scope of claim includes conditions reasonably identified by evidence
regulations.veteranTip: When you claim a condition, VA should also consider associated complications. For example, a spine claim should automatically consider associated radiculopathy.

regulations.title: Complete Claim Definition
regulations.summary: A complete claim requires: claimant's name, relationship to veteran, service information, signature, identification of benefit sought, and description of conditions.
keyPoints: For supplemental claims: must identify new and relevant evidence
For Higher-Level Review: must identify the decision date being reviewed
Must be signed by claimant or authorized person
regulations.veteranTip: Incomplete claims cause delays. Double-check you've provided everything required before submitting.

categories.title: VA's Duty to Assist (§3.159)
categories.description: What VA must do to help you with your claim

regulations.title: Competent Evidence Standards
regulations.summary: Defines competent medical evidence and competent lay evidence. Veterans are competent to report symptoms they personally observe.
keyPoints: Medical evidence requires qualified healthcare providers
Lay evidence: anything from someone with personal knowledge
Veterans ARE competent to report their own symptoms
Buddy statements are competent lay evidence
regulations.veteranTip: You don't need a doctor to say you have pain - you're competent to report that. But diagnosing WHY you have pain requires medical evidence.

regulations.title: Duty to Notify
regulations.summary: VA must notify you of what information and evidence is needed to substantiate your claim.
keyPoints: VA must tell you what evidence is missing
Must explain what VA will obtain vs. what you need to provide
Must send development letters for incomplete claims
regulations.veteranTip: If VA denies your claim without ever telling you what evidence was missing, they may have violated their duty to notify.

regulations.title: Duty to Assist in Obtaining Evidence
regulations.summary: VA must make reasonable efforts to obtain relevant records, both federal (service records, VA records) and non-federal (private medical records).
keyPoints: VA must request your service records
VA must obtain relevant VA treatment records
VA must try to get private records if you provide authorization
At least one follow-up request for non-federal records
regulations.veteranTip: If VA says they couldn't get your records, ask what efforts they made. They must make 'reasonable efforts' and document their attempts.

regulations.title: Medical Examinations
regulations.summary: VA must provide a medical examination when there's evidence of current disability, indication of association with service, and insufficient evidence to decide.
keyPoints: Required when: current disability + in-service event + indication of connection
Low threshold - need only 'indication' of connection
Must provide exam even for supplemental claims with new evidence
regulations.veteranTip: If VA denies without an exam, check if you met the low threshold for one. Having current symptoms + any in-service event usually triggers exam requirement.

categories.title: Service Connection Principles (§3.303-§3.310)
categories.description: The legal standards for connecting disabilities to service

regulations.title: Direct Service Connection
regulations.summary: Service connection may be granted for disability resulting from disease or injury incurred in or aggravated by active military service.
keyPoints: Three elements: current disability + in-service event + nexus
Must be incurred OR aggravated during service
Line of duty requirement (not due to misconduct)
regulations.veteranTip: For direct service connection, focus on documenting all three elements: (1) what you have now, (2) what happened in service, and (3) how they're connected.

regulations.title: Chronicity and Continuity
regulations.summary: For chronic diseases, service connection may be established by evidence of the disease in service and current manifestations. Continuity of symptoms can substitute for chronicity.
keyPoints: Chronic diseases shown in service with same condition now = service connected
Continuity: symptoms since service, even without formal diagnosis then
Lay evidence of continuous symptoms is valuable
regulations.veteranTip: If you've had symptoms continuously since service, document that timeline. Your lay statements about ongoing symptoms since discharge are important evidence.

regulations.title: Secondary Service Connection
regulations.summary: Disability which is proximately due to or the result of a service-connected disease or injury shall be service connected.
keyPoints: Your service-connected condition caused a new condition
Does NOT need to occur during service
Need medical evidence showing causation
regulations.veteranTip: Secondary conditions are powerful for increasing your rating. Think about what conditions your service-connected disabilities have caused - sleep apnea from PTSD, nerve damage from diabetes, hip problems from knee injuries, etc.

regulations.title: Aggravation by Service-Connected Condition
regulations.summary: Any increase in severity of a nonservice-connected disease caused by a service-connected disease or injury is secondary service connection.
keyPoints: Even aggravation (worsening) of another condition counts
VA rates the DEGREE of aggravation
Baseline severity established, then increase measured
regulations.veteranTip: If your service-connected condition made another condition WORSE (even if it didn't cause it), you may qualify for secondary service connection for the aggravation.

categories.title: Presumptive Service Connection (§3.307-§3.320)
categories.description: Conditions presumed service-connected based on service location or timing

regulations.title: Presumptive Service Connection - General
regulations.summary: Certain chronic diseases, tropical diseases, and conditions related to service are presumed service-connected if they manifest within specified periods.
keyPoints: Chronic diseases: must manifest to 10% within 1 year of discharge
Some diseases have longer presumptive periods
Presumption can be rebutted only by affirmative evidence
regulations.veteranTip: If you developed arthritis, heart disease, diabetes, or other chronic diseases within one year of discharge, they may be presumptively connected even without proving causation.

regulations.title: Diseases Subject to Presumption
regulations.summary: Lists specific diseases presumed service-connected for various veteran groups: chronic diseases, tropical diseases, POW diseases, and exposure-related conditions.
keyPoints: Chronic diseases list includes arthritis, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, etc.
Agent Orange presumptives for Vietnam veterans
Gulf War presumptives for Southwest Asia veterans
PACT Act added many new presumptives
regulations.veteranTip: Check the specific lists in §3.309 to see if your condition qualifies for presumptive connection based on when and where you served.

regulations.title: Gulf War Presumptives
regulations.summary: Compensation for Gulf War veterans with qualifying chronic disabilities: undiagnosed illnesses, medically unexplained chronic multi-symptom illnesses (like chronic fatigue, fibromyalgia, IBS).
keyPoints: Covers undiagnosed illnesses and chronic multi-symptom illnesses
Must have served in Southwest Asia theater
Includes chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, functional GI disorders
Disability must manifest to 10% or more
regulations.veteranTip: If you have unexplained symptoms after Gulf War service that doctors can't fully diagnose, you may still qualify for compensation under §3.317.

regulations.title: PACT Act - Toxic Exposure Presumptions
regulations.summary: Establishes presumptions for conditions related to toxic exposure, burn pits, radiation, and expanded Agent Orange coverage.
keyPoints: Burn pit exposure presumptives for Iraq/Afghanistan veterans
Expanded locations for Agent Orange presumption
Radiation-related cancers
Must have qualifying service
regulations.veteranTip: The PACT Act significantly expanded presumptive conditions. If you were denied before 2022, you may now qualify for presumptive connection.

categories.title: Effective Dates (§3.400)
categories.description: When your benefits start and how to protect back-pay

regulations.title: General Rule
regulations.summary: Effective date will be fixed according to facts found, but not earlier than the date of claim or the date entitlement arose, whichever is later.
keyPoints: Usually the date VA received your claim
Can be earlier with Intent to File
For increases: date of claim OR date entitlement arose (whichever later)
regulations.veteranTip: Your effective date is usually your claim date. That's why Intent to File is so important - it preserves an earlier date while you prepare your full claim.

regulations.title: Disability Compensation
regulations.summary: For direct service connection, effective date is day after discharge if claim filed within 1 year. Otherwise, date of claim.
keyPoints: Claim within 1 year of discharge = day after discharge effective date
Claim after 1 year = date VA received claim
Presumptive conditions: when requirements first met
regulations.veteranTip: If you're within 1 year of discharge, file NOW to get the earliest possible effective date (day after discharge). Every month you wait is lost back-pay.

regulations.title: Increased Ratings
regulations.summary: For increased ratings, effective date is date of claim or date entitlement arose, whichever is later. Can be up to 1 year before claim if increase is factually ascertainable.
keyPoints: Usually date of claim for increase
Can go back 1 year if medical evidence shows increase
Need evidence showing specific date condition worsened
regulations.veteranTip: For increases, gather medical evidence showing WHEN your condition got worse. If you can show the increase happened within the year before your claim, you might get earlier effective date.

regulations.title: Supplemental Claims
regulations.summary: For supplemental claims filed within 1 year of a decision, effective date can relate back to the original claim. After 1 year, date of supplemental claim.
keyPoints: Supplemental within 1 year: can get original claim date
Supplemental after 1 year: new claim date
Continuous pursuit preserves effective date
regulations.veteranTip: If you're filing a supplemental claim within 1 year of denial, you preserve your original effective date. Don't let the 1-year deadline pass!

categories.title: Review & Appeals (§3.2500-§3.2601)
categories.description: Your options when you disagree with a VA decision

regulations.title: Review Options
regulations.summary: After receiving notice of a decision, you have three review options: Supplemental Claim, Higher-Level Review, or Board Appeal. Must choose within 1 year to preserve effective date.
keyPoints: 1-year deadline from date of decision notice
Can choose different options for different issues
Supplemental Claim: add new evidence
Higher-Level Review: no new evidence, error review
Board Appeal: three dockets available
regulations.veteranTip: Don't just accept a denial. Review your options carefully: HLR if you think VA made an error with existing evidence, Supplemental if you have new evidence, Board if you want a judge to decide.

regulations.title: Supplemental Claims
regulations.summary: A supplemental claim allows you to submit new and relevant evidence for a previously decided claim. Filed on VA Form 20-0995.
keyPoints: Must include new and relevant evidence
New: not previously submitted
Relevant: relates to unestablished element
VA duty to assist reactivates with new evidence
regulations.veteranTip: The bar for 'new and relevant' is low. A nexus letter you didn't have before, buddy statements, updated treatment records - all can support a supplemental claim.

regulations.title: Higher-Level Review
regulations.summary: A senior reviewer examines whether VA made an error based on evidence in the record at time of decision. No new evidence allowed.
keyPoints: Review by more experienced adjudicator
No new evidence - only what was in record
Can request informal telephone conference
Good for clear errors in applying law
regulations.veteranTip: HLR is best when VA clearly misread your evidence or incorrectly applied the law. If you need to add new evidence, file supplemental instead.

regulations.title: Special Monthly Compensation Ratings
regulations.summary: Additional compensation beyond schedular ratings for: loss of use, blindness, deafness, being housebound, or needing aid and attendance.
keyPoints: SMC(k): loss of use of one hand, foot, eye, or creative organ
SMC(l): need for aid and attendance
SMC(s): housebound or 100% plus 60% additional
Higher SMC levels for more severe combinations
regulations.veteranTip: SMC is often overlooked! If you need help with daily activities, are essentially confined to home, or have lost use of limbs/organs, you may qualify for SMC on top of your rating.

regulations.title: Loss of Use
regulations.summary: Loss of use exists when a limb or organ has no effective remaining function. Does not require physical amputation.
keyPoints: Function must be so diminished that amputation would be equally serviceable
Applies to hands, feet, eyes, and creative organs
Each qualifies for SMC(k) rate
regulations.veteranTip: You don't need actual amputation. If your hand or foot is so non-functional that a prosthetic would work equally well, that's loss of use.

regulations.title: Aid and Attendance
regulations.summary: Additional allowance if you need regular aid and attendance of another person due to service-connected disabilities.
keyPoints: Inability to dress/undress, keep clean, attend to bathroom needs
Incapacity to protect self from hazards of daily environment
Being bedridden
Mental/physical incapacity requiring care or supervision
regulations.veteranTip: If someone helps you with bathing, dressing, eating, or you need supervision for safety, you may qualify for Aid and Attendance.

categories.title: Rating Protections (§3.344, §3.951)
categories.description: Rules that protect your ratings from reduction

regulations.title: Rating Stabilization
regulations.summary: Ratings in effect for 5+ years cannot be reduced unless sustained improvement is shown under ordinary conditions of life. Examination must be complete and full.
keyPoints: After 5 years at same rating, reduction requires sustained improvement
Must be improvement under ordinary conditions (not just in hospital)
Examination must be as complete as original rating exam
Applies to ratings based on diseases subject to improvement
regulations.veteranTip: If you've had a rating for 5+ years, VA can't reduce it just because one exam seems better. They must show SUSTAINED improvement in everyday life, not just test results.

regulations.title: Permanent Ratings
regulations.summary: Ratings for conditions likely to improve and in effect less than 5 years may be reduced based on any improvement. But 20-year ratings are protected.
keyPoints: Ratings under 5 years: standard for reduction
Ratings 5-20 years: stabilization protections apply
Ratings 20+ years: cannot be reduced except for fraud
regulations.veteranTip: If you've had your rating for 20 years, it's essentially permanent. VA cannot reduce it except in cases of fraud.

regulations.title: Total Disability Rating Protection
regulations.summary: A total rating (100%) in effect for 20 years is protected and cannot be reduced. TDIU held for 20 years is also protected.
keyPoints: 100% schedular rating for 20 years = permanent
TDIU for 20 years = protected at 100% rate
Only fraud can overcome this protection
regulations.veteranTip: If you've been at 100% (schedular or TDIU) for 20 years, that rate is protected for life. Document when your total rating began.

categories.title: VA Examinations (§3.326-§3.327)
categories.description: Rules governing C&P exams and reexaminations

regulations.title: Examinations
regulations.summary: When medical evidence is not adequate for rating purposes, VA will authorize an examination. Hospital reports and private examinations may be accepted.
keyPoints: C&P exam required when evidence is insufficient to rate
Private medical evidence can substitute if adequate
Hospital records from any government or private institution may be accepted
POW claimants must be offered VA hospital exam before denial
regulations.veteranTip: You don't always need a C&P exam. If your private doctor provides thorough documentation using DBQ format, it may be accepted.

regulations.title: Reexaminations
regulations.summary: Reexaminations may be scheduled when VA needs to verify continuing entitlement. Generally not required after age 55 unless improvement is likely.
keyPoints: Reexam when there's reason to believe condition changed
Not required for permanent disabilities
Generally not required after age 55
Must report to scheduled exams
regulations.veteranTip: If you're over 55 with a static condition, you likely won't be scheduled for routine reexams. But if you're younger, be prepared for occasional reexaminations.

regulations.title: Failure to Report for Examination
regulations.summary: If you fail to report for a scheduled exam without good cause, your claim may be denied or benefits reduced.
keyPoints: Original claims: rated on evidence of record (usually unfavorable)
Claims for increase: claim denied
Running awards: benefits may be reduced
Good cause exceptions exist
regulations.veteranTip: NEVER miss a C&P exam without notifying VA. If you can't make it, call immediately to reschedule. Missing exams is one of the most common reasons for denials.

criticalTimelines.importance: File within 1 year of discharge for earliest possible effective date (day after discharge)
criticalTimelines.consequence: Missing this deadline means your effective date will be your later claim date

criticalTimelines.importance: Choose a review option within 1 year to preserve your effective date in the review lane
criticalTimelines.consequence: After 1 year, you can still file supplemental claims but may lose earlier effective date

criticalTimelines.importance: File complete claim within 1 year of ITF to preserve that effective date
criticalTimelines.consequence: ITF expires and you'll need a new claim with new effective date

criticalTimelines.importance: Respond to proposed reduction letters within 60 days
criticalTimelines.consequence: Reduction may proceed without your input

criticalTimelines.importance: If requesting a Board hearing or submitting evidence, must elect within 120 days
criticalTimelines.consequence: May be limited to direct review docket

commonMistakes.mistake: Not filing Intent to File first
commonMistakes.impact: Losing months or years of potential back-pay
commonMistakes.solution: Always file ITF immediately, even before you have evidence ready

commonMistakes.impact: Claim denied or rated on incomplete evidence
commonMistakes.solution: Never miss exams; call to reschedule if you can't make it

commonMistakes.impact: Losing ability to preserve original effective date
commonMistakes.solution: File supplemental claim or HLR within 1 year of any denial
Most initial denials can be won on appeal with proper evidence

commonMistakes.impact: Leaving significant rating percentage on the table
commonMistakes.solution: Think about all conditions caused by your service-connected disabilities
Always respond with evidence and request hearing if needed
